blocks.title: Rules, the QP and batch evidence

summary.title: GMP and GDP
points: GMP: how medicines and APIs are made, tested and released. GDP: storage and transport afterwards.
EudraLex Vol. 4: Part I products, Part II APIs; Annex 15 validation, Annex 16 QP certification.
Legal principles: Directive (EU) 2017/1572; GDP guidelines cover wholesalers and transport.
Agencies inspect; passing sites get an EU GMP certificate published in EudraGMDP.
Every site in the dossier needs valid GMP status, for filing and for QP release.

exercises.scenario: A truck carrying released product sits at 35 °C for a day.

questions.prompt: Which rulebook governs this?
options: Annex 16 on QP certification
The quality agreement only
GMP Part II, which covers active substances in transit
GDP

questions.prompt: Where would you check that the Indian site's GMP certificate is current?
options: EudraVigilance, the EU safety database
EudraGMDP
The EUIPO register
The CoA of the last batch

exercises.scenario: The gap analysis shows a testing lab whose GMP certificate expired last year.

questions.prompt: What's the launch risk?
options: It can block filing and QP release
Only the artwork is affected
None, as long as the manufacturing site's certificate is valid and in date
Only a delay to the PSMF
questions.explanation: Every site named needs valid status.

questions.prompt: Which annex covers QP certification?
options: Part II
Annex 1
Annex 16
Annex 15

summary.title: The Qualified Person
points: No batch is sold in the EU until a QP certifies it; the QP is personally responsible.
Checks: made and tested per the licence under GMP; records reviewed; deviations closed or justified.
Also: results within specification; for imports, full EU testing done.
Certification is recorded in a register; QP qualifications are set by law and checked nationally.
QP certification is the last gate: send batch documents early.

exercises.scenario: The launch batch has one dissolution result outside specification, under investigation.

questions.prompt: Can the QP certify it now?
options: Yes, if the other results are well within their limits
Yes, because the CoA conclusion can be amended to 'complies'
No; it must be resolved through the quality system first
Yes, if management signs a waiver for the launch

questions.prompt: Who carries legal responsibility for the certification?
options: The MAH's general manager
The national agency that granted the licence
The manufacturer's head of production in India
The QP personally

exercises.scenario: The plan shows batch documents arriving at the QP two days before launch.

questions.prompt: What's wrong?
options: There's no time for QP review: the launch date is at risk
Nothing; QPs certify on the day the batch ships
Only the CoA is needed, and it takes minutes
The QP can sign before reading the records
questions.explanation: Give the QP the documentation early.

questions.prompt: For a batch from India, what extra must the QP see?
options: The updated PSMF and the QPPV's signature
The full analysis required on import
A new BE study on that batch
The artwork proof

summary.title: Specifications and the CoA
points: A specification lists tests, methods and limits; it's part of the licence, so changes need a variation.
A CoA reports one batch's results against the specification.
Release limits apply at release; shelf-life limits until expiry, sometimes wider.
Check batch number, every test present, results in limits, 'complies', signed and dated.
A CoA isn't QP certification; ask for launch and API CoAs as soon as testing ends.

exercises.scenario: You receive a CoA for launch batch B2301. The dissolution test is missing.

questions.prompt: What do you do?
options: Accept it, since dissolution is optional for a tablet that passed assay
Query it: every specification test must appear
Ask the wholesaler
Send it to the QP as is
questions.explanation: A complete CoA lists every test.

questions.prompt: An impurity is at 0.4%; release limit 0.3%, shelf-life limit 0.5%. Can the batch be released?
options: Yes, because 0.4% is below the 0.5% shelf-life limit
Yes: the shelf-life limit applies throughout
Only with a Type IA notification
No: at release, the release limit applies
questions.explanation: Wider shelf-life limits allow for growth over time.

exercises.scenario: The site wants to widen the assay limit to save a batch.

questions.prompt: What does that need?
options: Nothing, if the QP agrees
Only an internal change control
A variation, since the specification is part of the licence
Only a new CoA

questions.prompt: What does a CoA prove?
options: The batch's results meet the specification
The batch will stay within specification until its expiry date
The batch was made under GMP
The batch is released for sale in the EU
questions.explanation: It's an input to QP release.

summary.title: Stability and climatic zones
points: Stability studies justify the shelf life and storage instructions.
EU: zones I/II, 25 °C/60% RH. India: zone IVb, 30 °C/75% RH. Accelerated: 40 °C/75% for 6 months.
Harsher conditions can support an EU claim if they cover duration, enough batches and the marketed pack.
Missing EU-relevant data is one of the commonest gaps.
Data accrue in real time: file a shorter shelf life and extend by variation, or wait.

exercises.scenario: The dossier holds 6 months of data at 30 °C/75% RH in the marketed blister. You want 36 months.

questions.prompt: What's realistic?
options: A shorter shelf life now, extended later by variation
Run more accelerated studies to make up the time
36 months, since zone IVb data are harsher than the EU's
36 months, using the accelerated data alone
questions.explanation: Real-time data can't be accelerated after the fact.

questions.prompt: Could zone IVb data support an EU shelf life at all?
options: Only for the accelerated condition
No, only 25 °C/60% data count in the EU
Yes, if duration, batches and pack match the claim
Only for products made in the EU
questions.explanation: Harsher conditions can support the EU claim.

exercises.scenario: The site tested stability in a bottle, but you'll sell blisters.

questions.prompt: What's the problem?
options: Only the artwork needs to change
Data must come from the packaging actually sold
Bottle data are always accepted for blisters if the conditions were harsher
None; stability doesn't depend on packaging
questions.explanation: The pack protects against humidity differently.

questions.prompt: What does the accelerated condition do?
options: Set the storage instruction on the pack
Test the product in zone IVb
Replace long-term data for the full shelf life
Spot problems early, at 40 °C/75% for 6 months
questions.explanation: It complements, not replaces, long-term data.

summary.title: Validation
points: Validation is documented proof that a process, equipment or test works reliably.
Four kinds: equipment qualification, process, cleaning, analytical method.
Standard processes: a scheme in the dossier; commercial-scale validation after approval, before marketing.
Non-standard processes need validation data in the dossier.
Validation batches are often the launch batches: they sit on the supply critical path.

exercises.scenario: The dossier holds a process validation scheme for a standard tablet.

questions.prompt: When must validation be completed?
options: Before filing, with three batches in the dossier
After approval, before the product is put on the market
Within five years of launch, at the first renewal
Never; a scheme is enough for standard processes

questions.prompt: Which kind shows no residue carries over to the next product?
options: Analytical method validation
Equipment qualification
Process validation
Cleaning validation

exercises.scenario: The three validation batches are planned for the month before launch.

questions.prompt: Why does that sit on the critical path?
options: They're often the launch batches, and the QP must review the results
Validation batches can't be sold, so extra stock is needed later
They restart the DCP clock, because validation data are new information
The agency inspects each validation batch
questions.explanation: Timing and QP review both matter.

questions.prompt: A product uses a non-standard process. What's different?
options: Only cleaning validation applies
Validation happens after launch
Validation data are needed in the dossier itself
No validation is needed
questions.explanation: Only standard processes can defer it.

summary.title: Deviations, CAPA, change control
points: The quality system loops: record, investigate, correct, prevent, control changes.
Deviation: something didn't go as planned; investigation finds the cause and affected batches.
CAPA: corrective fixes this case, preventive stops recurrence.
Change control assesses and approves planned changes; it links to variations.
An open deviation can stop QP release; a change needing IB or II can't ship until approved.

exercises.scenario: During packaging of the launch batch, a step was done out of order.

questions.prompt: What's this?
options: A CAPA, closed once it's written down
A deviation to record and investigate
A change control to approve in advance
A variation to file with the agency

questions.prompt: What's the launch risk?
options: An open deviation can stop QP release
The licence is suspended
None, if the CoA says 'complies'
Only the artwork is affected
questions.explanation: Deviations must be closed or justified.

exercises.scenario: The site proposes moving tablet compression to a new building before launch.

questions.prompt: Which processes are triggered?
options: Nothing, if the equipment is the same
Only a deviation report
Only a CAPA, since a move inside the same site isn't a change
Change control, and probably a variation
questions.explanation: Change control is where quality meets regulatory.

questions.prompt: A temperature excursion keeps recurring. What does the 'P' in CAPA add?
options: A penalty for the responsible operator
A priority flag for the QP
Actions that stop it happening again
A pause in production

summary.title: Quality agreements in practice
points: A table of activities and parties: R does the work, A answers for it.
Key rows: EU release testing (usually the importer, for India) and change notification.
Change notification gives time to file variations before supply is hit.
Weak spots: vague notice periods, unclear stability ownership, no deviation timelines, no audit right.
Track it as a milestone: draft, agreed, signed. No agreement, no supply, no QP release.

exercises.scenario: Reviewing a draft quality agreement, you see 'changes will be notified in due course'.

questions.prompt: Why is that a problem?
options: The QP will spot every change during release anyway
It's fine; 'in due course' is the standard legal term
Unannounced changes can need variations that block supply
Only the PV agreement covers change notification
questions.explanation: Vague notice periods are a classic weak spot.

questions.prompt: Who usually does EU release testing for product from India?
options: The Indian manufacturer, before shipping
The wholesaler, on receipt
The national agency
The importer, or a lab on its behalf
questions.explanation: Full EU testing is needed on import.

exercises.scenario: Six weeks before first supply, the quality agreement is 'agreed but not signed'.

questions.prompt: What's the status for launch?
options: Not relevant to QP release
Still a blocker until signed
Only a PV issue
Done, since both sides agree on the text
questions.explanation: Draft, agreed, signed: only signed counts.

questions.prompt: Which missing clause could stop you checking the site's GMP yourself?
options: The audit right
The complaints row
The recall row
The stability programme row
questions.explanation: One of the common weak spots.

summary.title: Hot topics
points: Nitrosamines: possibly cancer-causing impurities; assess, test where at risk, meet EMA limits.
Elemental impurities: trace metals; ICH Q3D sets daily exposure limits.
Data integrity (ALCOA+): complete, accurate, traceable records.
Serious data-integrity findings can cost a site its GMP certificate for every product.
Ask for both assessments in gap analysis; check every site's inspection history.

exercises.scenario: An in-licensed dossier has a nitrosamine risk assessment from 2019.

questions.prompt: What's the issue?
options: None; nitrosamine assessments never expire once filed
It must be replaced by a stability study
It predates the EMA's 2020 review and is likely outdated
Only elemental impurities matter for generics
questions.explanation: A frequent gap in in-licensed dossiers.

questions.prompt: Which guideline sets limits for metal catalysts?
options: ICH Q3D
ICH M9
Annex 15
The QRD template

exercises.scenario: An inspection at your manufacturer finds backdated batch records.

questions.prompt: Which principle is breached?
options: Nitrosamine limits
Data integrity: contemporaneous, original records
The Bolar exemption
GDP storage and transport rules for released product

questions.prompt: Why could this hit more than your product?
options: The finding stays confidential
It only changes the CoA format
Only the inspected batch is affected
The site may lose its GMP certificate for everything it makes

summary.title: Rules, the QP and batch evidence
points: GMP covers making, testing and release; GDP covers storage and transport.
Valid GMP certificates (EudraGMDP) for every site are a filing and release condition.
The QP certifies each batch against the licence and GMP; it's the last gate.
Specifications are registered; the CoA reports a batch against them.
Stability under the right zone, duration and pack sets the shelf life you can claim.

exercises.scenario: Launch is in four weeks. You have the launch batch CoA, 12 months of EU-condition stability, and the site certificate expires next month.

questions.prompt: Which item is the biggest threat?
options: Nothing; all three are in order
The 12 months of stability, which is too short to launch on
The CoA, which should be issued by the QP
The expiring GMP certificate
questions.explanation: Valid GMP status is needed for QP release.

questions.prompt: What does the QP still need to see?
options: Batch records, closed deviations, results in spec, import testing
The marketing authorisation alone
Only the GMP certificate
Only the CoA, since it already summarises everything else

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a CoA and QP certification.
questions.modelAnswer: A CoA reports one batch's test results against the specification. QP certification is the QP's recorded, personal confirmation that the batch meets the licence and GMP, after reviewing the CoA, records and deviations; only then can it be sold.

exercises.scenario: A partner's stability data are all at 30 °C/75% RH in bottles; you'll sell blisters in the EU.

questions.prompt: What's the gap?
options: Only accelerated data count
The data don't cover the marketed pack
The conditions are too mild for the EU
Bottles always protect better, so it's fine
questions.explanation: Data must come from the packaging that will be sold.

questions.prompt: What's the realistic way forward if launch can't wait?
options: Skip stability and rely on the CoA
Ask the QP to approve a longer shelf life
Start blister studies and claim a shorter shelf life first
Claim 36 months from the bottle data

summary.title: Keeping quality under control
points: Validation proves processes, equipment, cleaning and methods work; launch batches often validate.
Deviations, CAPA and change control keep quality in a loop.
Changes to registered details need a variation before supply.
The quality agreement assigns release testing and change notification; it must be signed.
Nitrosamines, elemental impurities and data integrity can stop a launch late.

exercises.scenario: The manufacturer wants a new API supplier, and its last inspection had data-integrity findings.

questions.prompt: Which change processes are triggered?
options: Change control and very likely a variation
A deviation and a CAPA only
A new DCP, because the API source is part of the original assessment
Nothing until the next inspection

questions.prompt: Why do the inspection findings matter for your launch?
options: They change the specification limits
They only affect the API supplier
The site's GMP certificate, and every product, may be at risk
They are only relevant to GDP

questions.prompt: Name two weak spots to look for in a quality agreement and why each matters.
questions.modelAnswer: Vague change-notification periods: unannounced changes can need variations that block supply. A missing audit right: you can't check the site yourself. (Also: unclear stability ownership, no deviation-investigation timelines.)

exercises.scenario: Validation batches are also launch batches, and one has an open deviation.

questions.prompt: What's the effect?
options: The batch can ship, with the deviation closed later
QP release can't happen until it's closed or justified
None; validation batches are exempt
Only the stability study is delayed

questions.prompt: What should the PM put on the plan?
options: A new BE study on the batch with the open deviation
Nothing; quality owns it
A Type IA notification
The investigation's closure date, as a release dependency

summary.title: Quality: the whole picture
points: GMP and GDP cover the chain; every site needs valid GMP status.
The QP certifies each batch: last gate, personal responsibility.
Specifications are registered; CoAs show results; stability sets the shelf life.
Validation, deviations, CAPA and change control keep quality reliable.
Registered changes need variations; the quality agreement must notify them in time.
Check nitrosamines, elemental impurities and data integrity early.

exercises.scenario: You run the quality section of a gap analysis for an in-licensed Indian generic.

questions.prompt: Which three quality items do you ask for first?
options: The PSMF, the RMP and the QPPV's CV
Stability under EU conditions, nitrosamine assessment, site GMP status
The BE study, the trademark search and the FTO opinion
The artwork, the leaflet and the readability test

questions.prompt: The site's process validation is a scheme only. Is that a filing gap?
options: Not for a standard process; validation must finish before marketing
No, validation is never needed for generics
Yes, unless the QP waives it
Yes, validation data are always needed to file

questions.prompt: Which document must be signed before commercial supply?
options: The artwork approval
The PV agreement only
The FTO opinion
The quality agreement

exercises.scenario: Two weeks before launch, a batch has an out-of-spec result, and the site announces a new supplier.

questions.prompt: Can the batch be certified?
options: Yes, using shelf-life limits instead
Yes, if the CoA is reissued
No, not until the result is resolved
Yes, with a management waiver

questions.prompt: Can the new supplier's material go into launch stock?
options: Yes, if change control is open
Only once the needed variation is approved
Yes, after a 7-day notice to the agency and the QP
Yes, because the substance is the same
questions.explanation: IB or II must be approved before shipping.

questions.prompt: In two sentences, explain to management why quality issues so often move launch dates late.
questions.modelAnswer: QP certification is the last gate, so anything unresolved (an open deviation, a result out of spec, an expired GMP certificate, an unapproved variation) stops the batch right before shipping. Most of these can be found earlier, in gap analysis and by tracking quality milestones, which is the PM's job.
